At the heart of nearly every adjective use of "running" is one simple image: something that keeps going without stopping. Like a river that never pauses, something "running" is continuous, uninterrupted, or in constant motion. Keep this image in mind — it will make every meaning below feel intuitive.

1. Continuing over time, without a break

This is the most common use. When "running" describes something, it means that thing is ongoing — not a one-time event, but something that persists, recurs, or keeps happening.

  • A running battle — a conflict or disagreement that never fully ends; it keeps flaring up again and again. Politicians often have a running battle over tax policy for years.
  • A running joke — a joke that gets repeated among a group of people over a long period. Everyone in the friend group laughs at it every time it comes up, because it has a history.
  • A running commentary — a continuous, real-time description of something as it happens. A cricket commentator giving a ball-by-ball description of a match is giving a running commentary.
  • A running debate — a discussion or argument that people keep returning to without ever fully settling it.
  • A running total — a total figure that you keep updating every time new numbers come in. If you're tracking daily sales and you add each new sale to the previous sum throughout the day, you're keeping a running total.
  • Running costs (also called running expenses) — the regular, ongoing costs of keeping something in operation: electricity, salaries, maintenance. These are different from a one-time purchase cost. A business owner worries about running costs every single month.

The common thread: none of these things happen once and finish. They keep going.

2. One after another, with no gap in between (consecutively)

Here, "running" describes an unbroken sequence — things happening back to back, with no interruption in between.

This is special because, in this meaning, "running" almost always comes after the noun or number it describes, not before it.

  • "It rained for ten days running." — Ten consecutive days. No dry day in between.
  • "She won the championship three years running." — She won in year one, year two, and year three, without anyone else winning in between.
  • "He called me five times running." — Five calls, one after another.

Notice: you would say "five times running," not "five running times." The word sits at the end in this use. This is an important pattern to remember.

3. Flowing continuously (water or liquid)

When "running" describes water, it means water that is actively flowing — not sitting still in a tank or pool.

  • Running water — water that flows through pipes and comes out when you open a tap. This is considered a basic modern necessity. Many villages in developing areas lack running water and have to fetch it from wells or rivers.
  • A running stream — a stream that is currently flowing (as opposed to one that has dried up).
  • A running tap — a tap that has been left open and is actively releasing water.

4. Discharging fluid continuously (wounds, infections, the nose)

When a sore, wound, or nose is "running," it means it is producing and releasing liquid without stopping.

  • A running sore — a wound or infected area that keeps oozing or weeping fluid. It never dries and heals; it just keeps producing fluid. This phrase is also used figuratively: a "running sore" can mean a long-standing problem that causes ongoing pain and never gets resolved — like a territory dispute between two countries that has caused conflict for generations.
  • A running nose — you'll more often hear "runny nose," but "running nose" describes the same thing: a nose that keeps dripping mucus.

5. Currently operating or switched on (machines and engines)

"Running" can describe a machine or engine that is actively on and working at this moment.

  • "Don't reach into a running machine." — A machine that is currently in operation.
  • "She left the engine running." — The engine was left switched on.
  • "A running generator can be dangerous indoors." — A generator that is currently on and producing power.

6. Designed for or used in the sport of running

When placed before certain nouns, "running" describes things that exist for the purpose of the sport or activity of running.

  • Running shoes — shoes specifically designed for running.
  • Running track — a track where people run races.
  • Running gear — the clothing and equipment a runner uses.
  • Running club — a club whose members come together to run.

A small note: in this use, "running" is describing purpose ("made for running") rather than the idea of continuity. It's a slightly different flavour, but it's still used to modify a noun just like any adjective.

A few specific phrases built with "running" as an adjective come up so often that they deserve their own mention:

Running order — the sequence in which things are scheduled to happen. At a music festival, the running order tells you which band performs when, and in what sequence.

Running mate — in politics, the person who is chosen to run alongside a main candidate, usually for a lower office. When a party picks a presidential candidate, that candidate then picks a running mate to be the vice-presidential candidate. They run as a pair.

Running head (or running header) — in books, documents, or magazines, a line of text that appears at the top of every page, usually showing the book title or the chapter name. It "runs" across all the pages.

A running start — beginning something with momentum already built up. If you take a running start at a problem, you're not starting from zero; you've already done some preparation. Used both literally (running and jumping) and figuratively.
The One Thread That Ties It All Together

If you want a single anchor for your memory: "running" as an adjective almost always means something is in continuous, uninterrupted motion or activity — it doesn't stop, it keeps going.

Water keeps flowing → running water.
A fight keeps recurring → a running battle.
Days keep coming one after another → three days running.
A machine keeps operating → a running engine.
A wound keeps weeping → a running sore.

The image of a river — always moving, never pooling, never pausing — is the best mental picture you can carry for this word.
